This section continues my project by integrating modern deep learning methods and comparing them with traditional time-series models. I'll develop forecasting models, critically evaluate their performance, and reflect on how model choice influences forecasting accuracy and usefulness.

# Univariate Deep Learning Forecasting
::: {.panel-tabset}

**Data Preparation**
```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


# function part
def form_arrays(
    x,
    lookback=3,
    delay=1,
    step=1,
    feature_columns=[0],
    target_columns=[0],
    unique=False,
    verbose=False,
):
    # verbose=True --> report and plot for debugging
    # unique=True --> don't re-sample:
    # x1,x2,x3 --> x4 then x4,x5,x6 --> x7 instead of x2,x3,x4 --> x5

    # initialize
    i_start = 0
    count = 0

    # initialize output arrays with samples
    x_out = []
    y_out = []

    # sequentially build mini-batch samples
    while i_start + lookback + delay < x.shape[0]:

        # define index bounds
        i_stop = i_start + lookback
        i_pred = i_stop + delay

        # report if desired
        if verbose and count < 2:
            print("indice range:", i_start, i_stop, "-->", i_pred)

        # method-2: non-vectorized but cleaner
        indices_to_keep = []
        j = i_stop
        while j >= i_start:
            indices_to_keep.append(j)
            j = j - step

        # create mini-batch sample
        xtmp = x[indices_to_keep, :]  # isolate relevant indices
        xtmp = xtmp[:, feature_columns]  # isolate desire features
        ytmp = x[i_pred, target_columns]
        x_out.append(xtmp)
        y_out.append(ytmp)

        # report if desired
        if verbose and count < 2:
            print(xtmp, "-->", ytmp)
        if verbose and count < 2:
            print("shape:", xtmp.shape, "-->", ytmp.shape)

        # UPDATE START POINT
        if unique:
            i_start += lookback
        i_start += 1
        count += 1

    return np.array(x_out), np.array(y_out)

def history_plot(history):
    FS = 18  # FONT SIZE
    history_dict = history.history
    loss_values = history_dict["loss"]
    val_loss_values = history_dict["val_loss"]
    epochs = range(1, len(loss_values) + 1)

    # Plot all epochs
    plt.plot(epochs, val_loss_values, "r", label="Validation loss")
    plt.plot(epochs, loss_values, "bo", label="Training loss")
    plt.title("Training and validation loss")
    plt.xlabel("Epochs")
    plt.ylabel("Loss")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

    # Plot last 30 epochs
    plt.plot(epochs[-30:-1], val_loss_values[-30:-1], "r", label="Validation loss")
    plt.plot(epochs[-30:-1], loss_values[-30:-1], "bo", label="Training loss")
    plt.title("Training and validation loss (last epochs)")
    plt.xlabel("Epochs")
    plt.ylabel("Loss")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()


from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def regression_report(yt, ytp, yv, yvp):
    print("---------- Regression report ----------")

    # TRAINING METRICS
    print("TRAINING:")
    print(" MSE:", mean_squared_error(yt, ytp))
    print(" MAE:", mean_absolute_error(yt, ytp))

    # Training parity plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yt, ytp, "ro", markersize=3, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(yt, yt, "b-", linewidth=1)
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Actual y",
        ylabel="Predicted y",
        title="Training Parity Plot (perfect fit = blue line)",
    )
    plt.show()

    # Training time-series plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yt, "b-", label="Actual")
    ax.plot(ytp, "r--", label="Predicted", alpha=0.7)
    ax.legend()
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Index",
        ylabel="y(t)",
        title="Training: Time-Series Prediction",
    )
    plt.show()

    # VALIDATION METRICS
    print("VALIDATION:")
    print(" MSE:", mean_squared_error(yv, yvp))
    print(" MAE:", mean_absolute_error(yv, yvp))

    # Validation parity plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yv, yvp, "ro", markersize=3, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(yv, yv, "b-", linewidth=1)
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Actual y",
        ylabel="Predicted y",
        title="Validation Parity Plot",
    )
    plt.show()

    # Validation time-series
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yv, "b-", label="Actual")
    ax.plot(yvp, "r--", label="Predicted", alpha=0.7)
    ax.legend()
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Index",
        ylabel="y(t)",
        title="Validation: Time-Series Prediction",
    )
    plt.show()


# read csv
la_raw = pd.read_csv("data-raw/la_teu_data.csv", dtype=str)

# adjust data format
date_str = la_raw["Date"].str.strip()
date_str = date_str.str.replace(r"-(\d)$", r"-0\1", regex=True)
la_raw["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(
    date_str,
    format="%b-%y",
    errors="raise"
)

# handle the num-related columns
num_cols = [
    "Loaded_Imports",
    "Empty_Imports",
    "Total_Imports",
    "Loaded_Exports",
    "Empty_Exports",
    "Total_Exports",
    "Total_TEUs",
]

for col in num_cols:
    col_str = (
        la_raw[col]
        .str.strip()
        .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
    )
    la_raw[col] = pd.to_numeric(col_str, errors="coerce")

# Empty_Containers & Total_calc 
la_raw["Empty_Containers"] = (
    la_raw["Empty_Imports"] + la_raw["Empty_Exports"]
)

la_raw["Total_calc"] = (
    la_raw["Loaded_Imports"]
    + la_raw["Loaded_Exports"]
    + la_raw["Empty_Containers"]
)

la_raw["Total_TEUs"] = np.where(
    la_raw["Total_TEUs"].isna(),
    la_raw["Total_calc"],
    la_raw["Total_TEUs"],
)

#  sort& filter
la_teu = (
    la_raw
    .sort_values("Date")
    .loc[lambda df: df["Date"] >= pd.to_datetime("2000-01-01")]
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

# Create univariate series (Total TEUs)
t = la_teu["Date"].values                   
y = la_teu["Total_TEUs"].values.astype(float)

# log-transform to stabilize variance (similar to USD example)
x = np.log(y)
x = x.reshape(len(x), 1)

# Normalize the data
x_mean = np.mean(x, axis=0)
x_std = np.std(x, axis=0)
x = (x - x_mean) / x_std  # standardized Total TEUs
feature_columns = [0]
target_columns = [0]

print("Full series shape:", x.shape)
print("Date range:", t[0], "to", t[-1])

# Train / validation split
split_fraction = 0.75
cut = int(split_fraction * x.shape[0])

tt = t[0:cut]   # training dates
xt = x[0:cut]   # training data
tv = t[cut:]    # validation dates
xv = x[cut:]    # validation data

print("Training samples:", xt.shape[0])
print("Validation samples:", xv.shape[0])

# Mini-batch creation 
L = 12   # lookback window length
S = 1    # step
D = 1    # prediction delay

# training arrays
Xt, Yt = form_arrays(
    xt,
    lookback=L,
    delay=D,
    step=S,
    feature_columns=feature_columns,
    target_columns=target_columns,
    unique=False,
    verbose=False,
)

# validation arrays
Xv, Yv = form_arrays(
    xv,
    lookback=L,
    delay=D,
    step=S,
    feature_columns=feature_columns,
    target_columns=target_columns,
    unique=False,
    verbose=False,
)



print("---------- Data setup ----------")
print("training:", Xt.shape, Yt.shape)
print("validation:", Xv.shape, Yv.shape)

```

## Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
```{python}
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers, regularizers
from keras.layers import Dense, SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU, Dropout
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping
import numpy as np
from math import sqrt
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
import tensorflow as tf

import numpy as np
import random

tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)


# ========= SHARED HYPERPARAMETERS =========
loss_function = "MeanSquaredError"
learning_rate = 0.001
numbers_epochs = 250          
L1 = 1e-4                   
L2 = 1e-4
batch_size = 32         
input_shape = (Xt.shape[1], Xt.shape[2])
recurrent_hidden_units = 32

# early stop to prevent overfitting
early_stop = EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=10,
    restore_best_weights=True
)

def compute_rmse(y_true, y_pred):
    return sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))


# SIMPLE RNN MODEL
model_rnn = keras.Sequential()
model_rnn.add(SimpleRNN(
    units=20,
    activation='tanh',
    input_shape=input_shape,
    recurrent_regularizer=regularizers.L1(L1),
    return_sequences=False
))
model_rnn.add(Dropout(0.2))
model_rnn.add(Dense(
    units=1,
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L1L2(l1=L1, l2=L2),
    activation="linear"
))

print(model_rnn.summary())

opt = keras.optimizers.RMSprop(learning_rate=learning_rate)
model_rnn.compile(optimizer=opt, loss=loss_function)

history_rnn = model_rnn.fit(
    Xt,
    Yt,
    epochs=numbers_epochs,
    batch_size=batch_size,
    verbose=False,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop],
)

print("=== RNN: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_rnn)

Ytp_rnn = model_rnn.predict(Xt)
Yvp_rnn = model_rnn.predict(Xv)

print("=== RNN results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp_rnn, Yv, Yvp_rnn)
print("RNN Train RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yt, Ytp_rnn))
print("RNN Valid RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yv, Yvp_rnn))

Yvp_rnn_original = Yvp_rnn * x_std + x_mean  
Yvp_rnn_original = np.exp(Yvp_rnn_original)  

# 然后计算原始尺度的 RMSE
rmse_rnn_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(
    np.exp(Yv * x_std + x_mean), 
    Yvp_rnn_original
))
print(f"RNN RMSE (original scale): {rmse_rnn_original:.2f} TEUs")
```

## Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)
```{python}
from tensorflow.keras.layers import GRU, Dropout, Dense
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import regularizers
import numpy as np
import random
import tensorflow as tf

tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

model_gru = keras.Sequential()

model_gru.add(GRU(
    units=16,  
    activation='tanh',  
    recurrent_dropout=0.2,  
    dropout=0.2,  
    input_shape=input_shape,
    recurrent_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-4), 
    return_sequences=False
))

model_gru.add(Dropout(0.3)) 

model_gru.add(Dense(
    units=1,
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-4), 
    activation='linear'
))

opt_gru = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_gru.compile(optimizer=opt_gru, loss="mse")

history_gru = model_gru.fit(
    Xt, Yt,
    epochs=200,
    batch_size=8,            
    verbose=False,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop],
)

print("=== GRU: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_gru)

Ytp = model_gru.predict(Xt)
Yvp = model_gru.predict(Xv)

print("=== GRU results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp, Yv, Yvp)

from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

gru_train_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yt, Ytp))
gru_valid_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv, Yvp))

print("GRU Train RMSE:", gru_train_rmse)
print("GRU Valid RMSE:", gru_valid_rmse)

Yvp_gru_original = Yvp * x_std + x_mean         
Yvp_gru_original = np.exp(Yvp_gru_original)

Yv_original = np.exp(Yv * x_std + x_mean)

rmse_gru_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv_original, Yvp_gru_original))
print(f"GRU RMSE (original scale): {rmse_gru_original:.2f} TEUs")
```

## Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
```{python}
from tensorflow.keras.layers import LSTM, Dense
from tensorflow import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

model_lstm = keras.Sequential()

model_lstm.add(LSTM(
    units=12,
    activation='tanh',
    recurrent_activation='sigmoid',
    recurrent_dropout=0.25, 
    dropout=0.35,  
    input_shape=input_shape,
    recurrent_regularizer=regularizers.L1L2(l1=1e-4, l2=1e-4),  
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L1L2(l1=1e-4, l2=1e-4),
    return_sequences=False
))

model_lstm.add(Dropout(0.4))

model_lstm.add(Dense(
    units=1,
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-3),  #1e-4 → 1e-3
    activation='linear'
))

opt_lstm = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0003)  # 0.001 → 0.0003

model_lstm.compile(optimizer=opt_lstm, loss='mse')

early_stop_strict = EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=20,
    restore_best_weights=True,
    min_delta=0.005  
)

history_lstm = model_lstm.fit(
    Xt, Yt,
    epochs=300,  
    batch_size=32,  
    verbose=False,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop_strict],
)

print("=== LSTM: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_lstm)

# Predictions
Ytp_lstm = model_lstm.predict(Xt)
Yvp_lstm = model_lstm.predict(Xv)

print("=== LSTM results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp_lstm, Yv, Yvp_lstm)

# RMSE
lstm_train_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yt, Ytp_lstm))
lstm_valid_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv, Yvp_lstm))
print("LSTM Train RMSE:", lstm_train_rmse)
print("LSTM Validation RMSE:", lstm_valid_rmse)
Yvp_lstm_original = Yvp * x_std + x_mean
Yvp_lstm_original = np.exp(Yvp_lstm_original)

Yv_original = np.exp(Yv * x_std + x_mean)

rmse_lstm_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv_original, Yvp_lstm_original))
print(f"LSTM RMSE (original scale): {rmse_lstm_original:.2f} TEUs")
```

:::

### Analysis
#### 1. Relative Performance
Across the three deep learning models, the Simple RNN achieves the best overall performance, with the lowest validation RMSE (≈0.76) and the most stable prediction pattern. The GRU and LSTM models perform noticeably worse, with validation RMSE values above 0.90 and stronger deviation from the true series.

In terms of forecast behavior, the RNN is better able to follow the general upward trend and moderate fluctuations visible in the TEU series. GRU and LSTM, by contrast, tend to collapse toward the mean and fail to capture short-term variations, leading to flatter predicted curves and weaker correlation in the parity plots. These results suggest that for this relatively small dataset, simpler models generalize better than more complex gated architectures.

#### 2. Effectiveness of Regularization
Regularization played a crucial role in preventing overfitting.
For all models, dropout, early stopping, and weight decay were applied, and the training curves show relatively stable convergence without divergence between training and validation loss.

However, stronger regularization (especially in GRU/LSTM) often caused underfitting, flattening their predictions and shrinking their variance. This is a common issue when gated recurrent units are applied to small datasets: excessive regularization overwhelms the model’s capacity and leads to overly conservative predictions.

Overall, regularization improved training stability, but heavy regularization hurt the GRU/LSTM more than the RNN due to the dataset’s small size.

#### 3. Forecast Horizon
Based on the validation time-series plots, all three models show similar forecast limits.

- **Short-term (1–3 steps ahead):**

RNN predictions generally follow the direction of movement.

GRU and LSTM partially capture near-term changes but remain conservative.

- **Medium-term (3–6 steps ahead):**

All models begin to drift toward the mean.

Peaks and troughs are not accurately captured.

- **Long-term (>6 steps ahead):**

Models lose the seasonal and cyclical structure.

Predictions flatten significantly, especially in GRU/LSTM.

This indicates that these deep learning models are effective for short-horizon forecasting, but their ability to capture longer seasonal dynamics is limited when trained on a relatively small monthly dataset.

#### 4. Comparison with Traditional ARMA/ARIMA Models
Compared with the ARIMA model from Homework 3, the deep learning models display different strengths and weaknesses.

The seasonal ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,0,2)[12] model achieves a much lower RMSE (~66,959 TEUs on original scale) than the deep learning models (e.g., RNN ≈ 124,682 TEUs). ARIMA also produces more stable residuals and more accurate long-term seasonal forecasts.

- Deep learning models capture nonlinear short-term patterns better but fail to reproduce seasonal cycles due to limited data size and the lack of explicit seasonality structure.

- ARIMA models explicitly model monthly seasonality and cumulative trends, giving them a structural advantage for long-horizon forecasting.

- Deep learning models show higher variance in results, are more sensitive to hyperparameters, and require much larger datasets to outperform classical models.

Overall, for this dataset, ARIMA remains the superior model for long-term and seasonal forecasting, while RNN is the strongest deep learning model for short-term movement prediction, though still inferior to SARIMA in stability and accuracy. 

# Forecasting Performance Reflection
Across all univariate forecasting models I tested, the traditional SARIMA model achieved the strongest overall performance, with an RMSE of roughly 66,959 TEUs on the original scale. In contrast, the deep learning models—Simple RNN, GRU, and LSTM—showed noticeably higher validation errors, with RNN performing best among them (≈124,682 TEUs) and GRU/LSTM performing worse. These results highlight that model complexity does not necessarily translate into better predictive accuracy, especially when the dataset is relatively small and driven by strong linear and seasonal patterns.

Qualitatively, the choice of model strongly affects the usefulness of the forecast. SARIMA provides stable, interpretable predictions that respect the annual seasonal cycle of port activity, making it more reliable for short- and medium-term planning. Deep learning models, while more flexible and theoretically capable of capturing nonlinear structure, require far more data to generalize well. In this dataset, they tend to overfit the training window and produce less stable long-horizon forecasts.

The comparison taught me that forecasting is ultimately about matching the model to the structure of the data. For a dataset with a clear trend, strong seasonality, and limited sample size, a well-specified classical model can outperform more sophisticated neural networks. Deep learning remains valuable when incorporating richer exogenous factors or nonlinear behaviors, but for this univariate TEU series, SARIMA is the most appropriate tool.

## Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
```{python}
feature_columns = [0, 2]
target_columns  = [3]

L = 16  
S = 1
D = 1

Xt, Yt = form_arrays(
    xt,
    lookback=L,
    delay=D,
    step=S,
    feature_columns=feature_columns,
    target_columns=target_columns,
    unique=False,
    verbose=False,
)

Xv, Yv = form_arrays(
    xv,
    lookback=L,
    delay=D,
    step=S,
    feature_columns=feature_columns,
    target_columns=target_columns,
    unique=False,
    verbose=False,
)

print("training:", Xt.shape, Yt.shape)
print("validation:", Xv.shape, Yv.shape)

def compute_rmse(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true = np.array(y_true).reshape(-1)
    y_pred = np.array(y_pred).reshape(-1)
    return sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))

def regression_report(yt, ytp, yv, yvp):
    yt  = np.array(yt).reshape(-1)
    ytp = np.array(ytp).reshape(-1)
    yv  = np.array(yv).reshape(-1)
    yvp = np.array(yvp).reshape(-1)

    # TRAINING METRICS

    # Training parity plot

        xlabel="Actual y",

        title="Training Parity Plot (perfect fit = blue line)",
    )
    plt.show()

    # Training time-series plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yt, "b-", label="Actual")
    ax.plot(ytp, "r--", label="Predicted", alpha=0.7)
    ax.legend()
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Index",
        ylabel="y(t)",
        title="Training: Time-Series Prediction",
    )
    plt.show()

    # VALIDATION METRICS
    print("VALIDATION:")
    print(" MSE:", mean_squared_error(yv, yvp))
    print(" MAE:", mean_absolute_error(yv, yvp))

    # Validation parity plot
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yv, yvp, "ro", markersize=3, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(yv, yv, "b-", linewidth=1)
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Actual y",
        ylabel="Predicted y",
        title="Validation Parity Plot",
    )
    plt.show()

    # Validation time-series
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(yv, "b-", label="Actual")
    ax.plot(yvp, "r--", label="Predicted", alpha=0.7)
    ax.legend()
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Index",
        ylabel="y(t)",
        title="Validation: Time-Series Prediction",
    )
    plt.show()

loss_function = "MeanSquaredError"
learning_rate = 0.001
numbers_epochs = 250

    return_sequences=False
))
model_rnn_multi.add(Dropout(0.4))  
model_rnn_multi.add(Dense(
    units=1,
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(5e-4), 
    activation="linear"
))

opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0005)  
model_rnn_multi.compile(optimizer=opt, loss='mse')

early_stop_strict = EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=15,  # 10 → 15
    restore_best_weights=True,
    min_delta=0.005
)

history_rnn_multi = model_rnn_multi.fit(
    Xt, Yt,
    epochs=300,
    batch_size=32,
    verbose=0,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop_strict],
)

print("=== Multivariate RNN: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_rnn_multi)

Ytp_rnn_multi = model_rnn_multi.predict(Xt)
Yvp_rnn_multi = model_rnn_multi.predict(Xv)

print("=== Multivariate RNN results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp_rnn_multi, Yv, Yvp_rnn_multi)
print("Multivariate RNN Train RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yt, Ytp_rnn_multi))
print("Multivariate RNN Valid RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yv, Yvp_rnn_multi))


Yvp_rnn_multi_original = np.exp((Yvp_rnn_multi.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)

Yv_original = np.exp((Yv.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)

rmse_rnn_multi_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv_original, Yvp_rnn_multi_original))
print(f"Multivariate RNN RMSE (original scale): {rmse_rnn_multi_original:.2f} TEUs")


```

## GRU
```{python}
# ========================================
# MULTIVARIATE GRU MODEL
# ========================================

import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras.layers import GRU, Dense, Dropout
from tensorflow.keras import regularizers
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from math import sqrt

# Set random seeds for reproducibility
tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

# ========= HYPERPARAMETERS =========
loss_function = "MeanSquaredError"
learning_rate = 0.0005
numbers_epochs = 300
L1 = 1e-4
L2 = 1e-4
batch_size = 32
input_shape = (Xt.shape[1], Xt.shape[2])   # (12, 2) for lookback=12, features=2
recurrent_hidden_units = 16  # Smaller for multivariate to prevent overfitting

# Early stopping callback
early_stop = EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=15,
    restore_best_weights=True,
    min_delta=0.003
)

# ========= CREATE MODEL =========
model_gru_multi = keras.Sequential()

# ADD RECURRENT LAYER
model_gru_multi.add(GRU(
    units=recurrent_hidden_units,
    activation='tanh',  # tanh often more stable than relu for small datasets
    input_shape=input_shape,
    dropout=0.3,
    recurrent_dropout=0.3,
    recurrent_regularizer=regularizers.L2(5e-4),  # L2 for multivariate
    return_sequences=False
))

model_gru_multi.add(Dropout(0.35))

model_gru_multi.add(Dense(
    units=1, 
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(5e-4), 
    activation='linear'
))

# MODEL SUMMARY
print(model_gru_multi.summary())

# ========= COMPILING THE MODEL =========
opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=learning_rate, clipnorm=1.0)
model_gru_multi.compile(optimizer=opt, loss=loss_function)

# ========= TRAINING YOUR MODEL =========
history_gru_multi = model_gru_multi.fit(
    Xt,
    Yt,
    epochs=numbers_epochs,
    batch_size=batch_size,
    verbose=False,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop],
)

# ========= History plot =========
print("=== Multivariate GRU: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_gru_multi)

# ========= Predictions =========
Ytp_gru_multi = model_gru_multi.predict(Xt)
Yvp_gru_multi = model_gru_multi.predict(Xv)

# ========= REPORT =========
print("=== Multivariate GRU results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp_gru_multi, Yv, Yvp_gru_multi)

# ========= RMSE =========
print("Multivariate GRU Train RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yt, Ytp_gru_multi))
print("Multivariate GRU Valid RMSE:", compute_rmse(Yv, Yvp_gru_multi))

# ======= Restore to original scale: MULTIVARIATE GRU =======

Yvp_gru_multi_original = np.exp((Yvp_gru_multi.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)

Yv_original = np.exp((Yv.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)

rmse_gru_multi_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv_original, Yvp_gru_multi_original))
print(f"Multivariate GRU RMSE (original scale): {rmse_gru_multi_original:.2f} TEUs")

```

## LSTM
```{python}
from tensorflow.keras.layers import LSTM, Dense, Dropout
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import regularizers
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

loss_function = "MeanSquaredError"
learning_rate_lstm = 0.0005      
numbers_epochs_lstm = 300
batch_size_lstm = 32
lstm_units = 4                 
L1_lstm = 1e-4
L2_lstm = 1e-4

tf.random.set_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

model_lstm_multi = keras.Sequential()

model_lstm_multi.add(LSTM(
    units=8, 
    activation='tanh',
    recurrent_activation='hard_sigmoid', 
    input_shape=input_shape,
    dropout=0.4,  
    recurrent_dropout=0.4,
    recurrent_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-3),  
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-3),
    return_sequences=False
))

model_lstm_multi.add(Dropout(0.5))  

model_lstm_multi.add(Dense(
    units=1,
    kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-3),
    activation='linear'
))

opt_lstm = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0002, clipnorm=1.0) 
model_lstm_multi.compile(optimizer=opt_lstm, loss='mse')

early_stop_lstm = EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=30,  
    min_delta=0.005,  
    restore_best_weights=True
)

history_lstm_multi = model_lstm_multi.fit(
    Xt, Yt,
    epochs=350, 
    batch_size=32,
    verbose=0,
    validation_data=(Xv, Yv),
    callbacks=[early_stop_lstm],
)

print("=== Multivariate LSTM: Training history ===")
history_plot(history_lstm_multi)

Ytp_lstm_multi = model_lstm_multi.predict(Xt)
Yvp_lstm_multi = model_lstm_multi.predict(Xv)

print("=== Multivariate LSTM results on Port of LA Total_TEUs ===")
regression_report(Yt, Ytp_lstm_multi, Yv, Yvp_lstm_multi)

lstm_train_rmse = compute_rmse(Yt, Ytp_lstm_multi)
lstm_valid_rmse = compute_rmse(Yv, Yvp_lstm_multi)

print("Multivariate LSTM Train RMSE:", lstm_train_rmse)
print("Multivariate LSTM Valid RMSE:", lstm_valid_rmse)

# ======= Restore to original scale: MULTIVARIATE LSTM =======

Yvp_lstm_multi_original = np.exp((Yvp_lstm_multi.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)
Yv_original = np.exp((Yv.reshape(-1) * x_std) + x_mean)

rmse_lstm_multi_original = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(Yv_original, Yvp_lstm_multi_original))
print(f"Multivariate LSTM RMSE (original scale): {rmse_lstm_multi_original:.2f} TEUs")

```
:::

In the multivariate forecasting experiment, the three deep learning models—RNN, GRU, and LSTM—show clear differences in performance. Although all models use Imports and the USD Index to enhance short-term prediction of Total TEUs, the limited dataset (roughly 113 training points) constrains the ability of complex architectures to learn meaningful long-term dependencies. The simple RNN, with fewer parameters and lower model complexity, generalizes best and achieves the lowest validation RMSE, making it the strongest performer in this setting. GRU, despite having a more advanced gating mechanism, tends to overfit with such a small sample and therefore performs slightly worse than the RNN. LSTM, being the most parameter-heavy, overfits the most and delivers the weakest validation accuracy, producing overly smooth predictions that fail to capture true fluctuations. Overall, the results suggest that RNN is the most appropriate model for this dataset’s size and structure, while GRU and LSTM may only outperform it when trained on richer, larger, or more nonlinear multivariate datasets. This comparison highlights that in small-sample forecasting with moderate dynamics, simpler models can generalize more reliably than more complex deep learning architectures.

In this project, I compared traditional time-series models with deep learning architectures for forecasting Port of Los Angeles throughput. The results show a very clear pattern: traditional econometric models outperform all deep learning models by a large margin. The VAR model achieves the lowest RMSE on the original scale, followed by SARIMAX and ARIMAX, indicating that the relationship between TEUs, imports, exports, and macroeconomic indicators is highly linear and stable, making classical models particularly effective.

Deep learning performance depends strongly on the input structure. In the univariate setting, all neural networks perform poorly, with extremely high RMSE values—LSTM and GRU exceed 200,000 TEUs, showing that single-series learning does not capture the true drivers of port throughput. When multivariate inputs are included, the performance of neural networks improves substantially, with multivariate GRU and LSTM reducing RMSE by roughly 20–25%. However, even the best multivariate deep learning model remains significantly worse than the traditional VAR approach.

From a practical forecasting perspective, these results suggest that port throughput dynamics are dominated by linear interactions with economic variables rather than nonlinear temporal patterns. For real-world use, I would rely on the VAR model due to its accuracy, interpretability, and strong performance even with limited data. Deep learning models may still be useful if more high-frequency or nonlinear features are available, but with the current dataset, classical models clearly provide superior reliability. Overall, this comparison reinforces that model selection must be driven by data characteristics rather than complexity—a simpler model can be more effective when the underlying relationships are structurally linear and economically interpretable.
